findings.quote: on-demand is cheaper only when utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization)
findings.type: claims: link does not support the sentence (absolute word contradicted by the quote)
findings.evidence: Fact dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization, quote (CostOptimization_TableCapacityMode): "On-demand mode costs less for workloads with average provisioned capacity utilization below 35%. In many cases, even for workloads with provisioned capacity utilization higher than 35%, it can be more cost-effective to use on-demand mode especially if the workload has periods of low activity mixed with occasional peaks." The word 'only' is contradicted by the second sentence. The key stays right (steady use near 100%), but the explanation teaches a false rule. Rewrite without 'only' (for example: 'on-demand costs less when utilization is below 35%; this table runs near full use around the clock'). Note: changing the explanation of a verified question re-opens its verification.
findings.resolution: fix-28: dynamodb-q007 explanation only (stem, options and key byte-identical, same precedent as fix-18 lambda-q010): 'on-demand costs less when average utilization is [below 35%] or has quiet periods. This table runs near full use all day, so reserved capacity lowers the rate of the base load.' The word 'only' is gone; the quoted second sentence of the fact (quiet periods) is reflected.

findings.section: choose-it-or-not, table 'On-demand or provisioned capacity', row 'Long-term discount?'
findings.quote: None: reserved capacity is not for Standard-IA tables [or on-demand capacity mode](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-reserved-capacity-not-for-ia-on-demand)
findings.type: claims: outdated absolute claim; link supports less than the sentence
findings.evidence: The link supports only that reserved capacity is not for on-demand tables, not that no long-term discount exists. Saved AWS pages: savingsplans-userguide plan-types (full:savingsplans-userguide line 91): "Database Savings Plans provide flexibility to use AWS database services while reducing costs by up to 35% on Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Timestream, Neptune, Keyspaces, DMS, and Amazon OpenSearch Service. These plans automatically apply to the latest provisioned instance generations regardless of engine, instance family, size, Availability Zone (AZ), or Region, and also apply to serverless usage." and decision-guides (full line 2741): "most database and analytics services are now covered by Database Savings Plans (Amazon RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, ...)". 'None' is wrong for a reader who works at AWS. Fix: fetch https://aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/database-pricing/ through the tool, verify whether DynamoDB on-demand throughput is covered, and either register a fact and change the cell, or write 'No reserved capacity' instead of 'None'. Consider a Changed recently note (Database Savings Plans are new since 2022).
findings.resolution: fix-28: 'None:' replaced by 'No reserved capacity: it is not for Standard-IA tables [or on-demand capacity mode]', which the linked fact supports. Database Savings Plans: verified facts exist (dynamodb-faq-database-savings-plans-18-percent, dynamodb-database-savings-plans-cover-dynamodb), but no saved quote says whether on-demand throughput is covered (the FAQ says 'your Amazon DynamoDB usage'), so no Savings Plans claim was placed in the on-demand column.

findings.quote: On-demand is not always cheaper: it costs less when the average use of provisioned capacity would be [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization).
findings.type: claims: condition dropped from a fact
findings.evidence: Same quote as claims-02: AWS adds that above 35% on-demand "can be more cost-effective ... especially if the workload has periods of low activity mixed with occasional peaks", and the chapter's own Changed recently note (fact dynamodb-change-ondemand-price-cut-2024-11) says "most provisioned capacity workloads on DynamoDB will achieve a lower price with on-demand mode". Read alone, the sentence suggests 35% is a hard break-even. Add the clause: 'and often above it when traffic has quiet periods and peaks'.
findings.resolution: fix-28: 2-deep provisioned subsection now reads 'it costs less at average use [below 35%], and often above when quiet periods mix with peaks', the condition of the fact's second quoted sentence.

findings.quote: Traffic on a provisioned table with auto scaling jumps fivefold in ten seconds. What do clients see first? ... Throttled requests.
findings.type: technical: oversimplified answer, contradicted by a saved page
findings.evidence: full:amazondynamodb-developerguide (How DynamoDB auto scaling works): "Sudden, short-duration spikes of activity are accommodated by the table's built-in burst capacity." and (Burst capacity): "DynamoDB currently retains up to five minutes (300 seconds) of unused read and write capacity. During an occasional burst of read or write activity, these extra capacity units can be consumed quickly". The first thing clients see can be served requests from burst capacity; throttling follows when the spike lasts. Fix: ask 'What do clients see if the spike lasts several minutes?' or mention burst capacity (needs a fact).
findings.resolution: fix-28: Stop and answer rewritten: 'jumps fivefold and stays high for ten minutes. What do clients see?' Answer: 'Throttled requests, after [burst capacity] is spent and before auto scaling catches up' (verified fact dynamodb-burst-capacity-handles-spikes).

findings.section: in-one-breath, Figure caption (also diagrams/src/dynamodb-hero.json claim; data/28-dynamodb/speak.json dynamodb-s04 ten_second)
findings.quote: DynamoDB copies it to three Availability Zones before it confirms the write.
findings.type: claims: sentence says more than the fact
findings.evidence: Fact dynamodb-faq-sync-replication-three-azs: "DynamoDB synchronously replicates data across three Availability Zones (AZs) in an AWS Region, giving you high availability and data durability." Fact dynamodb-successful-write-http-200-durable: an HTTP 200 means the write "has been durably persisted". Neither quote says that all three copies exist before the acknowledgement. The same claim is in speak item s04: "Each record is copied to three Availability Zones before DynamoDB confirms it." Fix: 'DynamoDB replicates the item synchronously across three Availability Zones, and an HTTP 200 means the write is durable.'
findings.resolution: fix-28: hero spec claim and the 1-fast caption now say 'A write lands in the partition that the key's hash picks, and DynamoDB replicates it across three Availability Zones.' (no 'before it confirms'); diagram build dynamodb-hero re-rendered the SVG. Step 4 keeps the HTTP 200 durable fact. speak s04 ten_second: 'DynamoDB replicates each record across three Availability Zones, and a confirmed write is durable.'

findings.section: time-to-live-deletes-expired-items-without-using-write-capacity (also Say it, Stop and answer; 1-fast signals row 'no extra cost')
findings.quote: 3. **Delete later, for free.** ... > **Say it:** The short answer is: TTL deletes old items for free.
findings.type: technical: universal claim with a nearby exception
findings.evidence: docs/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/TTL lines 12-16: "The initial TTL delete does not consume Write Capacity Units (WCU) in the region in which the TTL expiry occurs. However, the replicated TTL delete to the replica table(s) consumes a replicated Write Capacity Unit when using provisioned capacity, or Replicated Write Unit when using on-demand capacity mode, in each of the replica regions and applicable charges will apply." The chapter teaches global tables, and Callvale's jobs table becomes a global table at stage 4 (STARTUP.md). Add 'in a single-Region table' or a Go deeper line, with a fact.
findings.resolution: fix-28: TTL step 3 is now 'Delete later, with no write units' and adds 'A global table is [charged for the replicated delete] in other Regions' (verified fact dynamodb-mrec-ttl-replicated-delete-charged). Say it and the Stop and answer say 'without write units' instead of 'for free'. The 1-fast signals row keeps 'no extra cost' only as a quoted stem phrase; its Because cell names write throughput.

findings.quote: A policy can [restrict access to individual items in a table](...) with `dynamodb:LeadingKeys`, a condition on [the partition key](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-leadingkeys-condition-key-partition-key).
findings.type: technical: condition dropped from a fact

The prose omits the modifier that makes the policy work; the chapter's own LeadingKeys card (back: 'dynamodb:LeadingKeys, with the ForAllValues modifier.') has it. Add 'with the ForAllValues modifier'. The exam signal at the end of the section has the same gap.

findings.quote: DynamoDB has [no user names or passwords](...); IAM policies decide every request.
findings.type: claims: unsupported clause, oversimplified
findings.evidence: The fact supports only 'no user names or passwords'. docs/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/access-control-resource-based: "DynamoDB supports resource-based policies for tables, indexes, and streams." and FAQ: "Yes, DynamoDB supports resource-based policies for tables and streams." Rewrite as 'IAM identity policies and resource-based policies on the table decide each request' with a fact, or drop the clause.
findings.resolution: fix-28: step 1 now says 'IAM policies decide each request. It also [supports resource-based policies for tables and streams]' (verified fact dynamodb-faq-resource-policies-tables-streams).

findings.quote: A relational database holds a connection and row locks per client, so one server sets the ceiling. [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections) and spreads items over partitions.
findings.type: claims: unsupported claim in an explanatory section
findings.evidence: No fact supports the first sentence; the link (lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections) supports only 'DynamoDB uses an HTTP API'. 'row locks per client' is inaccurate (locks are per row or transaction), and 'one server sets the ceiling' ignores read replicas and Aurora readers that chapters 26 and 27 teach. Rewrite with the Lambda fact's own wording (traditional database connections that need connection pooling), and link 'spreads items over partitions' to dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition.
findings.resolution: fix-28: the unsupported sentence ('row locks per client', 'one server sets the ceiling') is gone. New text: 'In a relational database, each client holds a connection, and updates to one row wait for its lock. [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API] with no open connection, and a key hash spreads items over partitions.' The hash mechanism is linked in hero step 2.

findings.quote: A bank wants backups that no administrator can delete, copied to a second account. ... AWS Backup, with a copy to that account and Vault Lock on the backup vault.
findings.type: technical: incomplete security answer
findings.evidence: docs/aws-backup/latest/devguide/vault-lock: "A vault locked in Governance mode can be managed or deleted by users who have the appropriate IAM permissions." and "A vault lock in Compliance mode cannot be altered or deleted by any user or by AWS." 'No administrator can delete' needs compliance mode. Add 'in compliance mode' (with a fact). Secure is the reader's weakest domain (45%).
findings.resolution: fix-28: answer now 'Vault Lock in compliance mode: that lock [cannot be altered or deleted by any user]' (verified fact backup-vault-lock-compliance-immutable-by-anyone).

findings.quote: In an Aurora global database, [only the primary cluster performs write operations](...), so the clusters in Europe and Asia cannot accept local writes.
findings.type: technical: overstated conclusion
findings.evidence: docs/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/WhatsNew: "Aurora global database write forwarding | You can now enable write capability on secondary clusters in a global database. With write forwarding, you issue DML statements on a secondary..." and aurora-global-database-connecting: "With write forwarding, Aurora automatically forwards the write statements to the w[riter]". Secondary clusters can accept writes and forward them; the writes still travel to the primary Region, which is why the option fails LOWEST latency. Rewrite: 'so every write still goes to the primary cluster's Region'. The fact's own scope notes write forwarding.
findings.resolution: fix-28: dynamodb-q022 option b why only (stem, options, key unchanged): 'so every write from Europe and Asia still travels to the primary cluster's Region.'

findings.quote: Time to live deletes each job record 90 days after the call.
findings.type: technical: contradicts the chapter's own TTL teaching
findings.evidence: Fact dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu: "DynamoDB automatically deletes expired items within a few days of their expiration time". The chapter's trap dynamodb-trap-ttl-deletes-on-time teaches exactly this. Write 'Time to live expires each job record 90 days after the call, and DynamoDB deletes it within a few days.'
findings.resolution: fix-28: decision now says 'Time to live expires each job record 90 days after the call.' (expiry, not deletion); the TTL subsection and fast trap teach the few-days delay.

findings.quote: | PITR | [Minimal RPO (seconds)](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-pitr-rpo-seconds) |

findings.evidence: Step 2 of the same section says the latest restore point is "five minutes before the current time" (fact dynamodb-pitr-restore-window-five-minutes-to-period), and the table says RPO seconds (fact dynamodb-dr-pitr-rpo-seconds). A reconciling clause needs a per-second restore fact and 2-deep sits at its blocking 4,500-word ceiling. Logged for the next revision.
